01 / The constraint

The constraint

EEG recordings can be too large to load into memory at once. The platform needed to ingest them, run analysis, export results and let a viewer request a short section of the signal.

02 / The implementation

What I built

I worked on a five-service platform with 50+ APIs. PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB hold structured data; Azure Blob Storage holds large files. Redis coordinates background jobs. The streaming path reads the requested time window rather than loading the whole recording. I also set up and ran the production and test environments on Azure: Docker Swarm services, CI/CD releases, versioned schema migrations and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring.

03 / A deliberate choice

The tradeoff

Heavy analysis runs outside the HTTP request. Object storage replaces local disk. Live viewing has to share resources with batch frequency-band analysis and EDF+/PDF export jobs, so those workloads are scheduled separately. A worker leases each job and sends heartbeats while it runs; if the heartbeats stop, an atomic requeue puts the job back, so a restart neither loses nor duplicates work.

04 / Evidence, with its limits

What the work showed

Bounded time-window streaming cancels stale requests when the viewer moves on. A binary format that groups values by column cut the payload per chunk from about 1.3 MB to 288 KB. Profiling took median (p50) first-chunk latency from roughly 2.2 s to 783 ms, and server send time from about 250 ms to 12 ms. Database fetches account for 87% of the remaining time. The sleep-analysis service processes a recording in memory-bounded chunks: a 24-hour recording went from 157.6 s to 32.6 s with identical results, and a 50-hour, 32-channel study completed. I led the investigation into a drift reported against a reference clinical viewer. Our traces matched the raw EDF recording at a correlation above 0.999; the drift was an 18.3% difference in display scale, not a sample delay.
